analysis.one_liner: Toughens safety rules for trains carrying hazardous materials, including two-person crews and hotbox detectors.
analysis.headline: The House never voted: the bill sat in subcommittee referral for the full two-year Congress while its Senate companion passed 68-30.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio derailment, this bill would require freight railroads to install defect-detecting sensors roughly every 10 miles on routes carrying hazardous materials, keep two crew members on most long freight trains, give state emergency officials advance notice of what hazardous chemicals are moving through their communities, and cut blockages at rail crossings. It would also raise the maximum fines for safety violations roughly tenfold, force older DOT-111 tank cars out of flammable-liquid service by May 2025, and nearly double federal grants for local first-responder hazmat training. It died in committee: the House held no markup and no vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work near rail lines, especially the towns and suburbs along routes carrying oil, ethanol, and toxic-by-inhalation chemicals; the train crews who would no longer run long hazmat trains alone; local fire departments and emergency planners who would get advance notice of what is coming through and larger federal training grants; and drivers stuck at blocked crossings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rail-line communities, train crews, first responders

how_it_helps.text: Requires every Class I railroad to install hotbox detectors — the sensors that catch wheel-bearing failures before derailments — along every 10-mile segment of track over which hazmat trains run, with federal standards for how alerts are handled [S3][S2].

Requires a minimum two-person crew (a certified conductor and engineer) on most freight trains, with no exceptions for trains hauling toxic-by-inhalation materials, long blocks of flammable tank cars, or trains over 7,500 feet [S3][S2].

Requires railroads and shippers to give state and Tribal emergency response officials advance notice and information — including gas discharge plans — about hazardous materials moving through their jurisdictions, and to reduce blocked rail crossings [S3][S2].

Raises maximum civil penalties for rail safety violations to the greater of $750,000-$1,750,000 or a percentage of the carrier's income, replacing fines as low as $25,000 that rarely changed railroad behavior [S3][S2].
Phases out DOT-111 tank cars — the older design involved in several fiery derailments — from flammable-liquid service by May 1, 2025, four years sooner than current law [S3][S2].

Imposes a $1 million annual fee on each Class I railroad and nearly doubles (from $2 million to $4 million) the cap on supplemental grants for local hazardous-materials first-responder training, and authorizes $27 million for defect-detector research and safer tank car development [S3][S2].

analysis.who_pays: The large Class I freight railroads, which would bear the cost of detectors, second crew members, higher fines, and a $1 million annual fee; and shippers who own older DOT-111 tank cars, who would need to retrofit or retire them. Some of those costs would likely flow into freight rates and the prices of shipped goods.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large freight railroads and hazmat shippers

drawbacks.text: The safety mandates are costly and the bill does not fund most of them: railroads would pay for detectors, doubled crews, and tank car retrofits, and the bill authorizes only $27 million in research spending that still requires a separate appropriation [S3].
Higher operating costs for railroads and shippers would likely be passed through to the prices of fuel, chemicals, and grain shipped by rail — a cost honest supporters would have to acknowledge.

The bill includes broad exemptions for smaller and low-speed railroads and lets the Transportation Secretary waive the crew requirement if an equivalent level of safety is shown, so its protections are deliberately narrower than a flat two-person mandate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to the public: fewer derailments like the one that forced evacuation of a town and contaminated its water, and firefighters who know what is on the train before they respond. The costs fall on a handful of very profitable freight railroads, some of which had cut crews and stretched train lengths in the years before the derailments. The main weakness is that key protections depend on future rulemaking by the Transportation Department and modest appropriations, so the bill's real-world effect would hinge on enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and sent to the Railroads subcommittee the next day, and then sat there with no markup, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Christopher Deluzio (D-PA), whose western Pennsylvania district borders the East Palestine derailment site, introduced the bill on March 21, 2023 together with Representative Nick LaLota (R-NY) [S3].

It was referred the same day to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Science, Space, and Technology Committee, and on March 22, 2023 to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials [S5][S1].
No further action of any kind was recorded for the remainder of the 118th Congress — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the Congress ended January 3, 2025 [S5].
It drew 17 cosponsors split nearly evenly between parties, 9 Republicans and 8 Democrats [S4].

A Senate companion Railway Safety Act passed the Senate 68-30 in 2023 with substantial Republican support, showing bipartisan appetite for rail safety rules that never translated into House action (widely reported; no provided source covers the Senate bill).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large freight railroads, which avoided the cost of detector installation, two-person crews, tank car phase-outs, and fines up to ten times larger. Rail-line communities and train crews gained nothing from the two years the bill sat without a vote.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Deluzio
for.role: Sponsor (D-PA); district adjoins the East Palestine derailment site
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Railway Safety Act of 2023 in the House on March 21, 2023 [S3].

for.name: Rep. Nick LaLota
for.what_they_did: Joined Deluzio in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start [S3].

for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill, nearly evenly split by party [S4].

for.name: Sens. Sherrod Brown and J.D. Vance
for.role: Lead sponsors of the Senate companion Railway Safety Act (S. 576)
for.what_they_did: Authored and steered the Senate version to a 68-30 passage in 2023, demonstrating bipartisan support the House version never got to test (widely reported; outside the provided record).

against.name: Rep. Sam Graves
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in his committee and its Railroads subcommittee for the entire 118th Congress with no markup or committee vote ever scheduled (widely reported; his chairship is public knowledge, the absence of action is on the congressional record) [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled floor time for any rail safety bill even after the Senate passed its companion 68-30 (widely reported; no provided source covers this).

against.name: Association of American Railroads / large freight railroads
against.role: Industry lobby for the Class I railroads
against.what_they_did: Opposed two-person crew mandates, defect-detector mandates, and higher penalties, arguing costs and automation benefits; their position was central to the bill going nowhere (widely reported; no provided source covers this).

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 9 of 17 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Senate companion passed 68-30 with many Republican votes — but no House vote was ever held, so party positions were never tested on the record.

industries.note: The bill would have required hotbox detectors every 10 miles on hazmat routes, minimum two-person crews, advance notice of hazmat shipments, blocked-crossing reductions, a $1 million annual fee per carrier, and penalties up to $1.75 million per violation. Avoiding all of that is what the industry got when the bill died in committee.

industries.industry: Hazmat shippers and DOT-111 tank car owners (oil, ethanol, chemicals)
industries.note: Owners of older DOT-111 tank cars would have had to retrofit or retire them by May 2025 and share notification duties with railroads. The cost is real, but it targets tank car designs repeatedly involved in fiery derailments.

industries.industry: Tank car manufacturers and retrofit shops
industries.note: Accelerating the DOT-111 phase-out creates demand for building and upgrading DOT-117-class cars — work the bill would also fund through a $5 million research program.

industries.industry: Local fire departments and emergency response training providers
industries.note: The bill nearly doubles the cap on federal hazmat first-responder training grants and funds them with a new $1 million annual fee on each Class I railroad rather than general taxpayer money.
